##Data Desciption
The data for this project came from the California Department of Public Health's COVID-19 Post-Vaccination Statewide Stats dataset. It contains information about COVID-19 cases, hospitalizations, and deaths among vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals in California from February 2021 through March 2023.

The original dataset contained 789 observations and 17 variables. The variables included the date, area, area type, the number of COVID-19 cases, hospitalizations, and deaths among vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals, the population sizes of both groups, and the corresponding rates per 100,000 people.

This was observational data collected from public health records, not data generated through randomized simulations. We used the existing data to compare COVID-19 rates between vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals.


## 1. Loading and Inspecting the Dataset
```{r}
covid <- read.csv("covid19postvaxstatewidestats.csv")
head(covid)
dim(covid)
str(covid)
```

## 2. Checking for Missing Values
```{r}
summary(covid)
```

```{r}
head(covid, 10)
```

```{r}
head(covid[, c("date",
               "unvaccinated_cases_per_100k",
               "vaccinated_cases_per_100k",
               "unvaccinated_hosp_per_100k",
               "vaccinated_hosp_per_100k",
               "unvaccinated_deaths_per_100k",
               "vaccinated_deaths_per_100k")], 10)
```

```{r}
covid[is.na(covid$unvaccinated_cases_per_100k),
      c("date",
        "unvaccinated_cases_per_100k",
        "vaccinated_cases_per_100k",
        "unvaccinated_hosp_per_100k",
        "vaccinated_hosp_per_100k",
        "unvaccinated_deaths_per_100k",
        "vaccinated_deaths_per_100k")]
```

This data set contains 6 missing values in each of the 6 rate variables. After looking at the first 10 rows, we can see that the missing values occur during the first six days of the data set (February 1-6, 2021). We were able to confirm that the remaining values contain all the variables necessary. These first six dates will be excluded from the analysis. 


## 3. Preparing the Dataset
```{r}
missing <- is.na(covid)
byrow_missing <- apply(missing, MARGIN = 1, sum)
covid_clean <- covid[byrow_missing == 0, ]

dim(covid_clean)
```
We cleaned the dataset by removing the first six rows because they contained missing values. The cleaned dataset contains 783 observations and 17 columns. We kept the original dataset unchanged.

## 4. Comparing Average Rates
The average rates were higher among unvaccinated individuals for COVID-19 cases, hospitalizations, and deaths. This suggests that vaccinated individuals experienced lower rates across all three measurements. These results support our hypothesis that vaccination is associated with lower COVID-19 rates.

```{r}
mean(covid_clean$unvaccinated_cases_per_100k)
mean(covid_clean$vaccinated_cases_per_100k)

mean(covid_clean$unvaccinated_hosp_per_100k)
mean(covid_clean$vaccinated_hosp_per_100k)

mean(covid_clean$unvaccinated_deaths_per_100k)
mean(covid_clean$vaccinated_deaths_per_100k)
```

## 5. Abstract
This project looks at the relationship between COVID-19 vaccination and COVID-19 cases, hospitalizations, and deaths in California. We used data from February 2021 through March 2023 to compare vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals. We cleaned the dataset by removing rows with missing values and compared the average daily rates per 100,000 people. We also used statistical tests to examine whether the differences between vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals were significant. Our results showed that unvaccinated individuals had higher average rates of cases, hospitalizations, and deaths. The statistical results provided strong evidence supporting these findings.

## 6. Executive Summary
1. This project examines the relationship between COVID-19 vaccination and cases, hospitalizations, and deaths in California.

2. Compared daily COVID-19 rates per 100,000 people between vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals.

3. We compared average daily rates per 100,000 people between vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals.

4. Unvaccinated individuals had higher average rates of COVID-19 cases, hospitalizations, and deaths.

5. Our findings suggest that vaccination was associated with lower COVID-19 rates.
